description: Every night you dream for about two hours. Most dreams fade when you wake up. Here is what science understands today about this mystery.

hero.hook: You dream about six years of your life. And you forget almost everything.

blocks.text: Every night, you spend about **two hours** dreaming. Over a lifetime, that's almost **six years**. However, when you wake up, most of these stories disappear within seconds.
Not all scientists agree on “why”. But they know better and better **when** we dream, and what the brain does during this time: it reorganizes memories, tests scenarios and digests emotions.

Sleep is not a complete turnoff. It advances by **cycles** of approximately **90 minutes**, several times per night. In each cycle, the brain goes through different phases: light sleep, deep sleep useful for recovering the body, then a very particular phase.

blocks.caption: During REM sleep, the eyes move under the eyelids.

blocks.text: This phase is called [[paradoxical sleep]]. The brain is almost as active as it is awake, but the body is paralyzed by the [[Muscle atonia]]. This is especially where long, narrative dreams are born. This paralysis prevents us from physically “playing” what we dream.
We dream **4 to 6 times** per night. We forget about **95 %** within ten minutes of waking up. If you remember a dream, it's often because you woke up right during it or right after it.

**Freud** thought that dreams mainly revealed hidden desires. Today, researchers prefer more concrete explanations, based on brain imaging, techniques that visualize brain activity. Dreaming especially activates the **limbic system**, the set of deep structures linked to emotions.

blocks.caption: During dreams, the brain works: emotions, images, memories.

blocks.text: Three main tracks dominate. First: **sort the memory**, keep the useful, let go of the rest. Second: **training for danger** in a world without real risk. Third: **digesting emotions**: during dreams, the brain revisits strong moments with less **norepinephrine**, a neurotransmitter linked to stress and wakefulness.

sections.title: What is the point of dreaming?

blocks.text: To store a memory permanently, the brain needs certain chemicals. However, during paradoxical sleep, the level of norepinephrine drops. Result: the dream remains in a very fragile memory.
As soon as you open your eyes, the light, sounds and thoughts of the day crush this fragile memory. The best way to keep it? Write down the dream **right away**, before even moving.
Before color television, few people said they dreamed in color. Today, most do. Our visual environment even influences the texture of our dreams.

sections.title: Why do we forget our dreams

blocks.text: Sometimes, we realize **that we are dreaming**, while remaining asleep: this is **lucid dreaming**. An area of ​​the brain linked to logic and self-reflection, the **prefrontal cortex**, then lights up a little.
Some can then influence the setting or transform a nightmare. Researchers are even studying this phenomenon to help athletes mentally repeat gestures, or to treat repetitive nightmares.

We dream especially during [[paradoxical sleep]], a phase when the brain is active and the body paralyzed. Dreaming probably helps to manage memory and emotions, even if we forget almost everything when we wake up.
